leaves.title: Verb be — singular: I and you
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn how to talk about yourself and one other person using the verb 'be' — the very first building block for introducing yourself in English.

Use 'am' with 'I' and 'are' with 'you':

• Full forms: I am / you are
• Contractions: I'm / you're
• Negative: I'm not / you aren't
• Question: Am I...? / Are you...?
• Short answers: Yes, I am. / No, I'm not. / Yes, you are. / No, you aren't.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to introduce yourself, say where you're from, and ask someone else simple questions about themselves.
examples: I am Diego. I'm from Mexico.
You are Sara. You're from Chicago.
Am I Marco? No, I'm Diego.
commonMistakes: Do not say 'I is' or 'you is' — use 'am' with I and 'are' with you.
Do not say 'Yes, I am not' as a short answer — say 'No, I'm not.'

leaves.title: Verb be — singular: he, she, and it
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn how to talk about other people and things — not just yourself — using 'he,' 'she,' and 'it.' This builds directly on what you already know about 'I' and 'you.'

Use 'is' with 'he,' 'she,' and 'it':

• Full forms: he is / she is / it is
• Contractions: he's / she's / it's
• Negative: he isn't / she isn't / it isn't
• Question: Is he...? / Is she...? / Is it...?
• Short answers: Yes, he is. / No, she isn't.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to describe a third person — a friend, a colleague, a place — the same way you already describe yourself.
examples: He is Marco. He's from Peru.
She is Sara. She's from Chile.
It is Lima. It's in Peru.
commonMistakes: Do not say 'he are' or 'she are' — use 'is' with he/she/it.
Do not forget the apostrophe in contractions: 'hes' is wrong, 'he's' is correct.

leaves.title: Verb be — plural: we, you, and they
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn how to talk about groups of people — including yourself as part of a group — using 'we,' 'you' (more than one person), and 'they.' Now that you can use 'be' for one person at a time, this extends the same idea to more than one.

Use 'are' with 'we,' 'you' (plural), and 'they':

• Full forms: we are / you are / they are
• Contractions: we're / you're / they're
• Negative: we aren't / you aren't / they aren't
• Question: Are we...? / Are you...? / Are they...?

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to talk about your team, your class, or a group of friends as a group, not just one person at a time.
examples: We are Marco and Sara. We're from Peru.
You are Ana and Leo. You're from Chile.
They are Tom and Lily. They're from Canada.
commonMistakes: Remember 'you' can be singular or plural, but the verb form is always 'are'.
Do not say 'they is' — always 'they are' or 'they're'.

leaves.title: Wh- and How questions with be
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn how to ask real questions with 'be' — not just yes/no questions, but questions that ask for information, like a name, a place, or an age. This is what you'll actually use to get to know someone.

Question words (who, what, where, when, how) come before the verb be:

• Where are you from?
• How old are you?
• Who is she?

We can contract 'is' after a question word (Where's he from?) but not after a pronoun at the end of the sentence (How old is he? — NOT How old's he?).

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to ask someone their name, where they're from, and how old they are — real conversation-starter questions.
examples: Where are you from? I'm from Toronto.
How old is she? She's ten.
What's your name? My name is Marco.
commonMistakes: Do not put the verb before the question word: 'Are where you from?' is wrong.
Do not contract 'is' when the sentence ends in a pronoun: 'Where is he?' NOT 'Where's he?'

leaves.title: Singular and plural nouns, a and an
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn how to talk about one thing versus more than one thing, and how to choose between 'a' and 'an' — two small words you'll use constantly.

There are three plural spelling patterns:

• Most nouns just add -s: a pencil → two pencils, a key → three keys
• Nouns ending in ch, sh, s, ss, or x add -es: a class → two classes, a watch → two watches
• Nouns ending in a consonant + y change y to i and add -es: a country → two countries

Use 'a' before a consonant sound and 'an' before a vowel sound (a, e, i, o, u):

• a book, a phone, a wallet
• an umbrella, an ID card, an orange

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to say whether you have one thing or several, and choose 'a' or 'an' correctly every time.
examples: I have a pencil and two pens.
She has an umbrella and three keys.
It's a photo, not an ID card.
commonMistakes: Don't forget the -s on plural nouns: 'two pencil' is wrong, 'two pencils' is correct.
Choose 'a'/'an' by the sound, not the spelling: it's 'an hour' (vowel sound) but 'a university' (consonant sound).
Don't just add -s to words ending in ch/sh/s/x or consonant+y: 'watchs' and 'countrys' are wrong — say 'watches' and 'countries'.

leaves.title: This, that, these, and those
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn how to point to things and say whether they're close to you or farther away — essential for shopping, showing photos, or describing what's around you.

The choice depends on two things: how many, and how close.

• this (singular, near you) — This is my bag.
• that (singular, farther away) — That is your bag.
• these (plural, near you) — These are my keys.
• those (plural, farther away) — Those are your keys.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to point out one or more things nearby or across the room and ask what they are.
examples: This is my phone. That is your phone.
These are new shoes. Those are old shoes.
What's this? It's a key chain.
commonMistakes: Don't use 'this'/'that' with plural nouns — say 'these keys', not 'this keys'.
'These'/'those' need a plural verb: 'These are nice', not 'These is nice'.

leaves.title: Possessive adjectives and possessive 's
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn how to say who something belongs to — a key skill for talking about your family, friends, and belongings.

Possessive adjectives go before a noun:

• I → my, you → your, he → his, she → her, it → its, we → our, you (plural) → your, they → their

For a person's name, add 's:

• Sara's brother, Tom's sister, my parents' house (plural noun ending in -s: add just an apostrophe)

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to talk about your own family and belongings, and ask who things belong to.
examples: This is my brother. His name is Leo.
That's Maria's daughter.
Is this your phone or her phone?
commonMistakes: 'It's' means 'it is'; the possessive form is 'its' with no apostrophe — 'The bag is nice. Its color is blue.'
Don't say 'the brother of Sara' as your default — 'Sara's brother' is the natural everyday form.

leaves.title: Adjectives: word order and form
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn where to put an adjective in a sentence and how adjectives behave differently from nouns in English.

An adjective goes before the noun it describes:

• a small car (NOT a car small)
• an expensive watch

Adjectives never take a plural -s, even when the noun is plural:

• good cars (NOT goods cars)
• blue keys (NOT blues keys)

An adjective can also come after the verb 'be':

• The car is fast. It's very expensive.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to describe things correctly, in the right word order, whether you're describing one thing or several.
examples: It's a beautiful photo.
They're good books.
This bag is cheap, but that one is expensive.
commonMistakes: Don't put the adjective after the noun: 'a watch small' is wrong.
Don't add -s to an adjective: 'goods watches' is wrong — say 'good watches'.

leaves.title: Simple present — affirmative and negative: I, you, we, they
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn how to talk about habits, routines, and things that are generally true — like what you usually eat or drink — using the simple present.

With I, you, we, and they, use the base form of the verb:

• I have breakfast at home.
• We eat a lot of fruit.

For the negative, use don't + base form:

• I don't drink coffee.
• They don't eat meat.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to say what you usually do and don't do, especially around everyday habits like eating and drinking.
examples: I have coffee every morning.
We don't eat breakfast at work.
They drink a lot of tea.
commonMistakes: Don't add -s to the verb with I/you/we/they: 'I haves' is wrong — say 'I have'.
Use 'don't', not 'not', for the negative: 'I not like fish' is wrong — say 'I don't like fish'.

leaves.title: Simple present — questions: I, you, we, they
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn how to ask yes/no questions and give short answers about habits and routines — building directly on the affirmative and negative forms you already know.

Use Do + subject + base verb:

• Do you live in London?
• Do they have a car?

Short answers use do/don't, not a repeat of the full verb:

• Yes, I do. / No, I don't.
• Yes, they do. / No, they don't.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to ask someone about their daily routines and habits, and answer the same questions naturally.
examples: Do you live near here? Yes, I do.
Do they live in Peru? No, they don't.
Do we have time for coffee? Yes, we do.
commonMistakes: Don't forget 'Do' at the start of the question: 'You live in London?' should be 'Do you live in London?'
Short answers don't repeat the main verb: 'Yes, I live' is wrong — say 'Yes, I do'.

leaves.title: Simple present — third person: he, she, it
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn how the simple present changes when you talk about one other person or thing — he, she, or it — instead of yourself or a group.

With he, she, and it, add -s to most verbs, following the same spelling rules as plural nouns:

• work → works (add -s)
• watch → watches, finish → finishes (add -es after ch, sh, s, ss, x)
• study → studies (consonant + y → -ies)

Three common verbs are irregular in this form: have → has, do → does, go → goes.

For the negative and question, use doesn't/does instead of don't/do, and the main verb goes back to its base form:

• She doesn't wear glasses. (NOT she doesn't wears)
• What does he do? Where does she work?

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to describe someone else's job, habits, and routine correctly in the third person.
examples: She works for a newspaper.
He doesn't wear glasses now.
What does she do? She's a teacher.
commonMistakes: Don't forget the -s on the verb with he/she/it: 'she work' is wrong — say 'she works'.
Don't add -s twice: 'she doesn't works' is wrong — say 'she doesn't work'.
have/do/go are irregular: 'she haves', 'he dos', and 'it gos' are all wrong — say 'has', 'does', 'goes'.

leaves.title: Adverbs of frequency
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn how to say how often you do something — not just what you do, but how regularly.

Common adverbs of frequency, from most to least often:

always, usually, sometimes, never

The adverb goes before the main verb, but after the verb 'be':

• I always get up at 7:00.
• I never drink coffee.
• She is usually tired in the morning.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to describe your routines and habits with more precision — not just 'I do X' but 'I always/usually/sometimes/never do X.'
examples: I always get up at seven in the morning.
He never eats breakfast.
We're usually tired on Mondays.
commonMistakes: Don't put the adverb before 'be': 'I always am tired' is wrong — say 'I am always tired.'
Don't put the adverb after the main verb: 'I get up always at 7:00' is wrong — say 'I always get up at 7:00.'
'Never' already makes a sentence negative, so it goes with an affirmative verb: 'He doesn't never eat meat' is wrong — say 'He never eats meat.'

leaves.title: Word order in questions: be and simple present
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll practice building correct questions from scratch, combining be-questions and do/does-questions — a skill for holding a real two-way conversation, not just answering.

Remember the two patterns:

• be-questions: (question word) + be + subject — Are you tired? What's your favorite day?
• simple-present questions: (question word) + do/does + subject + base verb — What do you do on Saturday? Does she work on Sunday?

Mixing these up is the most common word-order mistake at this level — check whether the sentence needs 'be' or 'do/does' before you build it.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to build both types of questions correctly, even when a question word is involved.
examples: What do you usually do on Saturday?
Are you tired on Sunday evening?
What time do you usually have lunch?
commonMistakes: Don't mix 'be' and 'do' in the same question: 'Do you are tired?' is wrong — say 'Are you tired?'
Don't forget 'do/does' with a simple-present question: 'What you do on Saturday?' is wrong — say 'What do you do on Saturday?'

leaves.title: Imperatives and object pronouns
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn how to give instructions with the imperative form, and how to replace a noun with a short object pronoun once it's already clear who or what you mean.

Imperatives use the base verb, with no subject:

• Be quiet, please. Sit down. Don't cry.

Object pronouns replace a noun that's the object of a verb:

• I → me, you → you, he → him, she → her, it → it, we → us, they → them

• Talk to me. Listen to them. Don't look at him.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to give simple instructions and avoid repeating a name or noun once your listener already knows who you mean.
examples: Open your books, please. Don't talk.
I love him, but he doesn't know it.
Listen to her. She's right.
commonMistakes: Don't use a subject pronoun in an imperative: 'You sit down' is less natural than just 'Sit down.'
Don't confuse subject and object pronouns: 'Talk to I' is wrong — say 'Talk to me.'

leaves.title: Can and can't
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn 'can' and 'can't' — used for both ability (what you're able to do) and permission (what's allowed) — two of the most useful words in everyday English.

can/can't + base verb, the same for every subject:

• I can drive. You can't park here. She can speak French.

Questions and short answers:

• Can you come on Monday? Yes, I can. / No, I can't.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to talk about what you're able to do, ask permission, and understand signs and rules that use can/can't.
examples: Can I park here? No, you can't.
She can speak Spanish.
Can you come at 10:00? Yes, I can.
commonMistakes: Don't add -s for he/she/it: 'she cans drive' is wrong — say 'she can drive'.
Don't use 'to' after can: 'I can to swim' is wrong — say 'I can swim'.

leaves.title: Like, love, and hate + verb + -ing
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn how to say how much you like or dislike an activity — not just a thing, but something you do.

After like, love, and hate, use verb + -ing when talking about an activity:

• I love cooking. I like reading. I hate cleaning.

Spelling rules for the -ing form:

• Most verbs just add -ing: read → reading
• Verbs ending in a silent e drop the e: drive → driving
• Verbs ending in one vowel + one consonant double the consonant: swim → swimming, shop → shopping

From most positive to most negative: love → like → don't like → hate.

Use don't/doesn't with like: I don't like camping. She doesn't like sports.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to talk about activities you enjoy and don't enjoy, with the right level of feeling.
examples: I love playing the piano.
He doesn't like traveling.
We hate cleaning.
commonMistakes: Use the base verb + -ing, not the infinitive, after these verbs in casual descriptions: 'I love to cook' is also correct, but 'I love cooking' is the more common everyday pattern taught here.
Don't forget don't/doesn't with 'like': 'She not likes it' is wrong — say 'She doesn't like it'.
Don't forget the spelling change: 'swiming' and 'driveing' are wrong — say 'swimming' and 'driving'.

leaves.title: Present continuous
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn a second present tense — the present continuous — used for things happening right now, at this exact moment.

Form: am/is/are + verb + -ing

• I'm making dinner. She's eating breakfast. They're reading.

Negative and question:

• I'm not working today. Is he sleeping? What are they doing?

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to describe what's happening right now, for yourself and for other people.
examples: I'm staying with my family this week.
She's eating breakfast right now.
What are they doing? They're watching a movie.
commonMistakes: Don't forget am/is/are — 'I working' is wrong — say 'I'm working'.
Don't drop the -ing ending: 'She's eat breakfast' is wrong — say 'She's eating breakfast'.

leaves.title: Present continuous or simple present?
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn how to choose between the two present tenses you now know — simple present and present continuous — a common source of confusion once you know both.

Use the simple present for habits, routines, and things that are generally true:

• He usually works in an office. She wears a suit every day.

Use the present continuous for something happening right now or a temporary situation:

• Today he's working in a hotel. Today she's wearing jeans.

Words like 'usually' and 'every day' signal simple present; 'right now' and 'today' signal present continuous.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to choose the correct present tense depending on whether you mean a habit or something happening now.
examples: He usually works in an office, but today he's working from home.
She usually wears a suit, but today she's wearing jeans.
I usually walk to work, but today I'm driving.
commonMistakes: Don't use the present continuous for a general habit: 'I'm working in an office' (as a permanent job description) is less natural than 'I work in an office'.
Don't use the simple present for something happening right now: 'I watch a movie now' is wrong — say 'I'm watching a movie now'.

leaves.title: There's a... / there are some...
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn how to say what exists or is present in a place — a room, a hotel, a city — without naming who owns it or where exactly it is yet.

Use there's/there is + a singular noun, and there are + some + a plural noun:

• There's a great view. There are some nice cafés nearby.

Negative and question use any, not some:

• There isn't a bathtub. Is there wi-fi? Are there any stores?

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to describe what a place has and doesn't have, and ask whether something is available.
examples: There's a room on the third floor.
There are two restaurants in the hotel.
Is there wi-fi? Yes, there is. Are there any elevators? No, there aren't.
commonMistakes: Use 'any', not 'some', in questions and negatives: 'There aren't some elevators' is wrong — say 'There aren't any elevators'.
Match singular/plural correctly: 'There's two restaurants' is wrong — say 'There are two restaurants'.

leaves.title: Simple past: be
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn the past tense of 'be' — your first step into talking about the past, and the foundation every other simple past form builds on.

Was/were forms:

• I/he/she/it was — you/we/they were

Negative: wasn't/weren't. Question: Was/Were + subject?

• Where were you at seven o'clock? I was at home. Were you alone? No, I wasn't.

There is/there are also has a past form: there was (singular) and there were (plural).

• There was a party at the school last night.

Common past time expressions: this morning, yesterday, last night, last week, last month, last year.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to say where you and others were at a specific past time, and ask the same about someone else.
examples: I was at home last night.
They weren't at school.
Were you at work yesterday? Yes, I was.
commonMistakes: Use 'was' with I/he/she/it, and 'were' with you/we/they — don't mix them up: 'I were' is wrong.
Don't add 'did' to a be-question: 'Did you were at home?' is wrong — say 'Were you at home?'

leaves.title: Simple past: regular verbs
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn how to talk about completed actions in the past using regular verbs — most English verbs follow this same simple pattern.

Four spelling patterns:

• Most verbs add -ed: work → worked, finish → finished
• Verbs ending in e add -d: live → lived, arrive → arrived
• Verbs ending in a consonant + y change y to i and add -ed: study → studied, cry → cried
• Verbs ending consonant-vowel-consonant double the final consonant: stop → stopped, prefer → preferred

Negative and question use didn't/did + the base verb, for every subject:

• We didn't rent a car. Did they arrive on time? Yes, they did.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to describe completed past actions and events using regular verbs correctly.
examples: We rented a house near the university.
They didn't invite everyone.
Did you pack your suitcase? Yes, I did.
commonMistakes: Don't forget -ed in the affirmative: 'We rent a house last year' is wrong — say 'We rented a house last year'.
Don't add -ed after didn't/did: 'We didn't arrived' is wrong — say 'We didn't arrive'.
Don't just add -ed to a consonant+y verb: 'studyed' and 'cryed' are wrong — say 'studied' and 'cried'.

leaves.title: Simple past irregular verbs: get, go, have, do
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn the past forms of four extremely common irregular verbs — they don't follow the -ed pattern, so their past forms must be learned individually.

• get → got, go → went, have → had, do → did

Negative and question still use didn't/did + the base form, just like regular verbs:

• I didn't go to school today. Did you have breakfast? Yes, I did.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to describe your day using these four very frequent irregular verbs correctly in the past.
examples: I got up at 6:00 and got a taxi.
We went to school and had lunch there.
I did my homework, but I didn't do the housework.
commonMistakes: Don't say 'goed', 'getted', 'haved', or 'doed' — these verbs are irregular: went, got, had, did.
The base form returns after didn't/did: 'I didn't went' is wrong — say 'I didn't go'.

leaves.title: Simple past: more irregular verbs
leaves.lessonBody:
In this lesson, you'll learn eight more common irregular past forms, building on 'get,' 'go,' 'have,' and 'do' — with practice choosing correctly between regular and irregular verbs together.

More irregular past forms:

• buy → bought, leave → left, say → said, see → saw, send → sent, sit → sat, tell → told, write → wrote

There's no shortcut for irregular verbs — they simply need to be memorized, one at a time, through practice.

By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to use these eight verbs correctly in the past, alongside regular verbs, in real sentences about your own experiences.
examples: I bought a new book and saw a movie.
She sat next to me and told me her name.
I left my phone at home and sent an email instead.
commonMistakes: Don't regularize irregular verbs: 'buyed', 'seed', 'sitted', and 'writed' are all wrong — the correct forms are bought, saw, sat, wrote.
'Said' is pronounced /sɛd/, not like 'paid' — it's an irregular pronunciation as well as an irregular spelling.
